body.heading: Why breathing reaches stress so quickly
paragraphs: Stress speeds the body up: heart, muscles, breath. Most of that system is automatic, but breathing sits at a useful border — it runs itself, yet you can also steer it. Slow the breath down, especially the out-breath, and you send the rest of the system a signal it understands: the emergency, if there was one, is easing.
This is not about breathing “correctly” or achieving some special state. It is about using the one dial you can reach to influence the ones you cannot.

body.heading: A simple pattern to borrow
paragraphs: Try this for a minute or two: breathe in through your nose for a slow count of four, and out for a count of six, as if fogging a mirror gently. Let the out-breath be the long, lazy part. If counting irritates you, just make each out-breath a little longer than the one before.

Shoulders down, jaw unclenched, hands loose. If you feel light-headed, you are trying too hard — breathe smaller and more normally. The goal is “a bit slower than stress wants,” nothing more dramatic.

body.heading: Use it at the seams of the day
paragraphs: Breathing practice works best sprinkled rather than saved for crises: before opening a difficult email, in the parked car, while the kettle boils, in the queue. Small, regular use builds the skill so it is actually available on the day you really need it.
And if stress in your life is heavy and constant, breathing room is a support, not a solution — pair it with the people and professionals who can help with the causes, not just the symptoms.

takeaway: Slow the out-breath, soften the shoulders, and let the rest of the system take the hint.
